extracted.intended_audience: researchers and authors deciding where to submit manuscripts (especially business scholars and students)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a scholarly journal is predatory or trustworthy when choosing where to submit a manuscript. Includes red flags, recommended checklists, and organizational memberships to verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: General characteristics of predatory journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Predatory journals are generally thought to be journals that exhibit deceptive, unethical, or exploitative publishing practices. This often includes a questionable peer-review process, a pay-to-publish model, and a lack of transparency and quality control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an umbrella definition: look for combinations of deception, exploitation, lack of transparency, and poor quality control rather than a single failing. The article cites the OMICS FTC case as an example of deceptive practices (misleading peer review, publishing fees, false impact factors and indexing claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of little or no peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: In spite of peer review claims, evidence of very little peer review or none at all. A clearly stated peer review policy may also be lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the journal's stated peer-review process and look for concrete evidence it is actually followed (timelines that are unrealistically short, acceptance emails without substantive reviewer reports, or absence of reviewer information). If peer review is unclear or absent, treat the journal with suspicion.

rubrics_metrics.name: False claims of indexing
rubrics_metrics.description: False claims of indexing in research databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check indexing claims against the named databases (e.g., Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed) rather than relying solely on the journal's website. Some predatory journals list bogus or irrelevant indexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: False or misleading impact factors/metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: False claims of impact factor or misleading metrics that are not acceptable practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm any impact factor or metric with the authoritative source (e.g., Clarivate's Journal Citation Reports). Watch for made-up metrics or metrics from obscure services that mimic legitimate ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-disclosure of author fees until after submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-disclosure of author fees required to publish until after an article is submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A trustworthy journal will clearly state any article processing charges (APCs) or other fees up front in author instructions. Surprise fees after submission are a red flag for exploitative/predatory practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial board concerns (minimal disclosure or unauthorized listing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial board with minimal information disclosed. The editorial board members may also be listed without their knowledge or permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for full names, affiliations, and verifiable contact information for editors. If in doubt, contact listed editorial members to confirm their association. Lack of transparency or fake/misrepresented editors is a warning sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish predatory vs. low-quality vs. legitimate open-access
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of the challenge lies in distinguishing predatory journals from journals that are simply low quality. It is also important to recognize the increasing number of legitimate open-access journals where authors must pay a fee to retain copyright and make their work freely available, versus pay-to-publish predatory journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate journals case-by-case rather than assuming all APC-charging journals are predatory. Consider peer-review rigor, editorial practices, transparency, and membership in reputable organizations when making distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Think. Check. Submit. checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Think. Check. Submit. website and checklist developed to assist researchers to determine whether a journal is trustworthy or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think. Check. Submit. is produced with support from COPE and others; it provides practical checklist questions to assess trustworthiness but does not itself make definitive determinations about specific journals. Use it as a structured evaluative tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify publisher membership in COPE
rubrics_metrics.description: Check a publisher’s membership in the Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE). Members follow the highest standards of publication ethics and apply COPE principles of publication ethics outlined in the core practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership in COPE indicates commitment to core practices and 'Principles of Transparency and Best Practice in Scholarly Publishing.' Use membership as one positive indicator, but confirm the journal adheres to COPE practices in actuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify publisher membership in OASPA
rubrics_metrics.description: Check a publisher’s membership in the Open Access Scholarly Publishers Association (OASPA). Members undergo a strict initial review procedure and must continue to exemplify high standards to maintain membership in OASPA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OASPA membership suggests the publisher meets recognized open-access standards. As with other memberships, treat this as supporting evidence rather than a sole determinant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cabells' blacklist indicators and categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Cabells Scholarly Analytics maintains a subscription-based 'blacklist' of predatory and deceptive academic journals. Cabells uses 60 indicators to identify deceptive, fraudulent, or predatory practices. The indicators include questions of integrity, peer review, publication practices, indexing/metrics, fees, and other areas that are categorized as severe, moderate, or minor indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If accessible, use Cabells' criteria as a comprehensive diagnostic framework. The multi-indicator approach and severity categorization can help prioritize which issues are most serious when evaluating a journal.
